newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korea Telecom sees foreign shareholders from 1998.
newsitem.headline: Korea Telecom sees foreign shareholders from 1998.

text.p: The South Korean government is considering plans to allow foreigners to buy shares in the nation's giant telephone utility by 1998, a senior company executive said on Thursday.

Lee Sang-ho, director of Korea Telecom's privatisation department, said the government would also cut a planned sale of its stake to the public by half to seven percent this year because of the stock market's doldrums.
"The original plan was 14 percent for this year, but because the stock market was not doing well, the plan was cut in half," Lee told a UBS Securities Investor Forum in Seoul.
He added that the public listing of shares of Korea Telecom, the world's ninth largest telecommunications network in terms of installed lines, would be delayed to 1997.

Currently, foreign investors cannot purchase shares in the telephone service provider. But the government has made proposals to the World Trade Organisation to allow foreigners access to the shares by January 1, 1998, Lee said.

The government currently holds 80 percent, or 230 million shares, of Korea Telecom's shares. The government has said it plans to reduce its holding to 51 percent, the minimum stake required under current regulations.
The expected sell-off of millions of Korea Telecom's shares has cast a shadow over the bourse on fears that they would swamp an already supply-heavy market, brokers said.

The Seoul stock market has tumbled almost 19 percent since the end of April, when the composite index was at 980.90, on fears that the economy was on the road to a deepening slowdown. The index closed Thursday at 797.57.
Korea Telecom's Lee, acknowledging those concerns, said: "Investors who want to buy these shares may sell off other stock to raise funds," pressuring the market further.
"The government doesn't want to rock the boat so much, so it is being careful," he said.
Seoul began selling shares in Korea Telecom to the public in 1993. It had planned to list the utility in 1995, but delayed the plan due to concerns about the impact on the stock market.
Korea Telecom shares are seen as very attractive because of its dominance on the lucrative telecommunications market and government-backed stability.
The telephone giant currently enjoys a monopoly on local service, a whopping 92 percent of the domestic long-distance market, and a 76 percent share of international service.

Telecommunications is one of the nation's fastest growing sectors, with total revenue for telephone service growing to $7.95 billion in 1995 from $4.3 billion in 1990, according to information ministry data.
Under pressure from world trade bodies, South Korea is striving to deregulate the telecommunication industry.
This year, it licensed 27 new service providers in sectors such as personal communication services, international long-distance and wireless data communications.

From 1998, foreign firms will be able to directly compete on the domestic front. They will also be able to buy stakes of up to 30 percent of most South Korean telecommunication companies in all service sectors.
Separately, a Dacom Corp executive told the conference he expected to see the company's net profit rising to 20 billion won ($24.3 million) in 1996 on sales of 650 billion.
Dacom, a Korea Telecom spin-off, posted a net profit of 13.5 billion won in 1995 on a revenue of 370 billion won.
"The growth will come primarily from the addition of our domestic long-distance service," said Cho Yong-wan, Dacom's director of finance. Dacom launched the service in January.
(Conversion: $1 = 822 won)
